what_it_does: Modern processors include a small, very fast buffer called a micro-op cache (uop cache) that stores pre-decoded, ready-to-execute versions of frequently used instructions, saving the cost of re-decoding them from scratch every time. Data center programs — web servers, databases, key-value stores — miss this cache constantly because their instruction footprints are large. Standard cache-eviction policies (like 'throw out the item that was used least recently') were designed for data caches where every miss costs roughly the same; in a uop cache, a miss can be disproportionately expensive because the CPU must re-fetch and re-decode a whole group of instructions, and sometimes only part of a group is cached (a 'partial hit') which still wastes work. FLACK is a new offline eviction policy — meaning it is computed with hindsight, seeing the full access sequence — that correctly accounts for these variable and unequal miss costs, giving a tighter 'how good could we possibly do' benchmark than the classical Belady's algorithm (which assumes all misses cost the same). FURBYS is then a practical online policy that approximates FLACK in real hardware by using pre-collected instruction profiles to distinguish permanently useful entries from those that are only briefly hot, and ignoring entries that the profile says rarely pay off when making eviction decisions.
